report:
**Conclusion: No—current best evidence does not support coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) for improving Parkinson’s movement symptoms or slowing motor decline.**

An early small trial (80 people, 2002) suggested high-dose CoQ10 (up to 1200 mg/day) might slow functional decline on UPDRS, generating optimism: https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/782965. However, the definitive phase 3 QE3 randomized trial in early Parkinson disease was stopped early for futility and reported CoQ10 was safe/well tolerated but showed **no evidence of clinical benefit**: https://read.qxmd.com/read/24664227/a-randomized-clinical-trial-of-high-dosage-coenzyme-q10-in-early-parkinson-disease-no-evidence-of-benefit. Independent summaries reached the same conclusion—that research into CoQ10 for PD effectively ended after QE3 showed no clinical benefit: https://www.michaeljfox.org/news/coenzyme-q10-study-shows-no-clinical-benefit. Major guidance for Parkinson’s management does not recommend CoQ10 as a motor treatment: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71.

**Bottom line:** CoQ10 appears generally safe, but it should not be used to treat tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, balance problems, or to modify PD progression. Patients should prioritize proven therapies (levodopa/dopaminergic drugs, exercise/physiotherapy, and specialist care) and discuss supplements with their neurologist because CoQ10 can interact with medicines such as warfarin and may add cost without benefit.
